Description: Current artificial intelligence systems exhibit characteristic failure modes: context-bounded memory loss, inability to navigate previously failed reasoning paths, and the absence of genuine structural self-evaluation. This paper argues that these failures are not incidental engineering limitations but consequences of a fundamental architectural gap: current AI systems are built without reference to the foundational laws governing information. Drawing on the three foundational laws of the Special Theory of Everything (SToE) — the Law of Information Conservation, the Law of Connection, and the Law of Autoinjection — we derive the specific architectural requirements that a genuinely information-native AI system must satisfy. We describe the required vessel: a persistent reasoning graph in which no information point is discarded, a topology-aware navigation mechanism distinct from similarity-based retrieval, and a structural self-evaluation loop grounded in autoinjection.

Description: This paper introduces autoinjection as a formally distinct class of mathematical mapping not present in the classical taxonomy established by the Bourbaki group. Classical set theory recognizes three classes of functions — injection, surjection, and bijection — based on how elements of a domain correspond to elements of a codomain treated as external to the domain. Autoinjection is defined as a mapping in which the codomain is a subset of the domain itself, such that the output of a function is an element of its own input set. This property, which classical mathematics treats as paradoxical or pathological, is here proposed as a fundamental and well-defined structural class. The formal definition, basic properties, and relationship to existing mathematical structures are presented. The implications for self-referential systems, recursive structures, and the foundations of set theory are discussed.

Description: This paper introduces autoinjection as a formally distinct class of mathematical mapping not present in the classical taxonomy established by the Bourbaki group. Classical set theory recognizes three classes of functions — injection, surjection, and bijection — based on how elements of a domain correspond to elements of a codomain treated as external to the domain. Autoinjection is defined as a mapping in which the codomain is a subset of the domain itself, such that the output of a function is an element of its own input set. This property, which classical mathematics treats as paradoxical or pathological, is here proposed as a fundamental and well-defined structural class. The formal definition, basic properties, and relationship to existing mathematical structures are presented. The implications for self-referential systems, recursive structures, and the foundations of set theory are discussed.

Description: Current artificial intelligence systems exhibit characteristic failure modes: context-bounded memory loss, inability to navigate previously failed reasoning paths, and the absence of genuine structural self-evaluation. This paper argues that these failures are not incidental engineering limitations but consequences of a fundamental architectural gap: current AI systems are built without reference to the foundational laws governing information. Drawing on the three foundational laws of the Special Theory of Everything (SToE) — the Law of Information Conservation, the Law of Connection, and the Law of Autoinjection — we derive the specific architectural requirements that a genuinely information-native AI system must satisfy. We describe the required vessel: a persistent reasoning graph in which no information point is discarded, a topology-aware navigation mechanism distinct from similarity-based retrieval, and a structural self-evaluation loop grounded in autoinjection.

Description: This paper introduces autoinjection as a formally distinct class of mathematical mapping not present in the classical taxonomy established by the Bourbaki group. Classical set theory recognizes three classes of functions — injection, surjection, and bijection — based on how elements of a domain correspond to elements of a codomain treated as external to the domain. Autoinjection is defined as a mapping in which the codomain is a subset of the domain itself, such that the output of a function is an element of its own input set. This property, which classical mathematics treats as paradoxical or pathological, is here proposed as a fundamental and well-defined structural class. The formal definition, basic properties, and relationship to existing mathematical structures are presented. The implications for self-referential systems, recursive structures, and the foundations of set theory are discussed.

Description: Current artificial intelligence systems exhibit characteristic failure modes: context-bounded memory loss, inability to navigate previously failed reasoning paths, and the absence of genuine structural self-evaluation. This paper argues that these failures are not incidental engineering limitations but consequences of a fundamental architectural gap: current AI systems are built without reference to the foundational laws governing information. Drawing on the three foundational laws of the Special Theory of Everything (SToE) — the Law of Information Conservation, the Law of Connection, and the Law of Autoinjection — we derive the specific architectural requirements that a genuinely information-native AI system must satisfy. We describe the required vessel: a persistent reasoning graph in which no information point is discarded, a topology-aware navigation mechanism distinct from similarity-based retrieval, and a structural self-evaluation loop grounded in autoinjection.

The Law of Information Conservation holds that no information point vanishes from reality — it can only lose connections with other information points. The Law of Autoinjection holds that everything, including the information field itself, is an information point, with no exterior to the system. Description: Current artificial intelligence systems exhibit characteristic failure modes: context-bounded memory loss, inability to navigate previously failed reasoning paths, and the absence of genuine structural self-evaluation. This paper argues that these failures are not incidental engineering limitations but consequences of a fundamental architectural gap: current AI systems are built without reference to the foundational laws governing information. Drawing on the three foundational laws of the Special Theory of Everything (SToE) — the Law of Information Conservation, the Law of Connection, and the Law of Autoinjection — we derive the specific architectural requirements that a genuinely information-native AI system must satisfy. We describe the required vessel: a persistent reasoning graph in which no information point is discarded, a topology-aware navigation mechanism distinct from similarity-based retrieval, and a structural self-evaluation loop grounded in autoinjection.

Description: This paper introduces autoinjection as a formally distinct class of mathematical mapping not present in the classical taxonomy established by the Bourbaki group. Classical set theory recognizes three classes of functions — injection, surjection, and bijection — based on how elements of a domain correspond to elements of a codomain treated as external to the domain. Autoinjection is defined as a mapping in which the codomain is a subset of the domain itself, such that the output of a function is an element of its own input set. This property, which classical mathematics treats as paradoxical or pathological, is here proposed as a fundamental and well-defined structural class. The formal definition, basic properties, and relationship to existing mathematical structures are presented. The implications for self-referential systems, recursive structures, and the foundations of set theory are discussed.

Description: Current artificial intelligence systems exhibit characteristic failure modes: context-bounded memory loss, inability to navigate previously failed reasoning paths, and the absence of genuine structural self-evaluation. This paper argues that these failures are not incidental engineering limitations but consequences of a fundamental architectural gap: current AI systems are built without reference to the foundational laws governing information. Drawing on the three foundational laws of the Special Theory of Everything (SToE) — the Law of Information Conservation, the Law of Connection, and the Law of Autoinjection — we derive the specific architectural requirements that a genuinely information-native AI system must satisfy. We describe the required vessel: a persistent reasoning graph in which no information point is discarded, a topology-aware navigation mechanism distinct from similarity-based retrieval, and a structural self-evaluation loop grounded in autoinjection.

Description: This paper introduces autoinjection as a formally distinct class of mathematical mapping not present in the classical taxonomy established by the Bourbaki group. Classical set theory recognizes three classes of functions — injection, surjection, and bijection — based on how elements of a domain correspond to elements of a codomain treated as external to the domain. Autoinjection is defined as a mapping in which the codomain is a subset of the domain itself, such that the output of a function is an element of its own input set. This property, which classical mathematics treats as paradoxical or pathological, is here proposed as a fundamental and well-defined structural class. The formal definition, basic properties, and relationship to existing mathematical structures are presented. The implications for self-referential systems, recursive structures, and the foundations of set theory are discussed.

Description: Current artificial intelligence systems exhibit characteristic failure modes: context-bounded memory loss, inability to navigate previously failed reasoning paths, and the absence of genuine structural self-evaluation. This paper argues that these failures are not incidental engineering limitations but consequences of a fundamental architectural gap: current AI systems are built without reference to the foundational laws governing information. Drawing on the three foundational laws of the Special Theory of Everything (SToE) — the Law of Information Conservation, the Law of Connection, and the Law of Autoinjection — we derive the specific architectural requirements that a genuinely information-native AI system must satisfy. We describe the required vessel: a persistent reasoning graph in which no information point is discarded, a topology-aware navigation mechanism distinct from similarity-based retrieval, and a structural self-evaluation loop grounded in autoinjection.

Description: Current artificial intelligence systems exhibit characteristic failure modes: context-bounded memory loss, inability to navigate previously failed reasoning paths, and the absence of genuine structural self-evaluation. This paper argues that these failures are not incidental engineering limitations but consequences of a fundamental architectural gap: current AI systems are built without reference to the foundational laws governing information. Drawing on the three foundational laws of the Special Theory of Everything (SToE) — the Law of Information Conservation, the Law of Connection, and the Law of Autoinjection — we derive the specific architectural requirements that a genuinely information-native AI system must satisfy. We describe the required vessel: a persistent reasoning graph in which no information point is discarded, a topology-aware navigation mechanism distinct from similarity-based retrieval, and a structural self-evaluation loop grounded in autoinjection.

Description: Current artificial intelligence systems exhibit characteristic failure modes: context-bounded memory loss, inability to navigate previously failed reasoning paths, and the absence of genuine structural self-evaluation. This paper argues that these failures are not incidental engineering limitations but consequences of a fundamental architectural gap: current AI systems are built without reference to the foundational laws governing information. Drawing on the three foundational laws of the Special Theory of Everything (SToE) — the Law of Information Conservation, the Law of Connection, and the Law of Autoinjection — we derive the specific architectural requirements that a genuinely information-native AI system must satisfy. We describe the required vessel: a persistent reasoning graph in which no information point is discarded, a topology-aware navigation mechanism distinct from similarity-based retrieval, and a structural self-evaluation loop grounded in autoinjection.

Description: Current artificial intelligence systems exhibit characteristic failure modes: context-bounded memory loss, inability to navigate previously failed reasoning paths, and the absence of genuine structural self-evaluation. This paper argues that these failures are not incidental engineering limitations but consequences of a fundamental architectural gap: current AI systems are built without reference to the foundational laws governing information. Drawing on the three foundational laws of the Special Theory of Everything (SToE) — the Law of Information Conservation, the Law of Connection, and the Law of Autoinjection — we derive the specific architectural requirements that a genuinely information-native AI system must satisfy. We describe the required vessel: a persistent reasoning graph in which no information point is discarded, a topology-aware navigation mechanism distinct from similarity-based retrieval, and a structural self-evaluation loop grounded in autoinjection.

Description: This paper presents the three foundational laws of the Special Theory of Everything (SToE): the Law of Information Conservation, the Law of Connection, and the Law of Autoinjection. First introduced in Voronin (2021) and developed across subsequent work, these laws are here stated explicitly and systematically for the first time. The Law of Information Conservation holds that no information point vanishes from reality — it can only lose connections with other information points. The Law of Autoinjection holds that everything, including the information field itself, is an information point, with no exterior to the system. Together these three laws constitute a formal foundation for SToE and generate specific, testable consequences for artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and the foundations of mathematics.

Description: This paper presents the three foundational laws of the Special Theory of Everything (SToE): the Law of Information Conservation, the Law of Connection, and the Law of Autoinjection. First introduced in Voronin (2021) and developed across subsequent work, these laws are here stated explicitly and systematically for the first time. The Law of Information Conservation holds that no information point vanishes from reality — it can only lose connections with other information points. The Law of Connection holds that connections between information points are created exclusively by observers or creators. The Law of Autoinjection holds that everything, including the information field itself, is an information point, with no exterior to the system. Together these three laws constitute a formal foundation for SToE and generate specific, testable consequences for artificial intelligence, cognitive science, and the foundations of mathematics.
